strengths: Extensive and diverse theory: the paper combines a clean (if elementary) singularity/geometry result, an EYM-based loss decomposition into optimization vs. rank-bias error, PAC-Bayes bounds with explicit complexity ratio, and a non-trivial argument transferring deterministic rank-sensitive Gaussian complexity bounds (Pinto et al. 2025) to the Bayesian posterior-mean predictor via a convex-hull/closure invariance argument (Appendix E). This last contribution is the most original and technically substantive piece of the theory.

Broad empirical coverage across three architecture families (MLP, LSTM, Transformer) and four data modalities (tabular/clinical, time-series, text, plus MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/toy regression in the appendix), each with an OOD shift dataset, giving a reasonably comprehensive picture of when low-rank BNNs help.

Thorough related-work positioning (Appendix A) that carefully differentiates the method from mean-field VI, low-rank covariance approximations, rank-1 perturbations, and Bayesian LoRA/SVGD variants along axes of parameterization, posterior support, and training regime (end-to-end vs. post-hoc).

High reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, architecture specs, hardware/software configuration, random seeds, and an explicit variance-preserving initialization scheme (Appendix F) with derivations, plus SVD-based initialization from pretrained weights.

Candid discussion of limitations, including the persistent calibration gap vs. Deep Ensembles, need for hyperparameter tuning (rank, KL weight), overlapping confidence intervals for some metrics, and the explicit acknowledgment that the empirical Gaussian complexity bounds are vacuous (Fig. 3) despite being theoretically interesting.
The consistent calibration–OOD detection tradeoff identified across all three main experiments is a genuine, reproducible empirical finding that is discussed thoughtfully rather than cherry-picked.
weaknesses: The headline theoretical result (Theorem 3.4, posterior singularity) is a straightforward consequence of the pushforward of any distribution under a rank-reducing polynomial map landing on a measure-zero set; the proof is correct but conceptually minor, and the paper's framing/title ('Singular Bayesian Neural Networks') gives this elementary fact outsized prominence relative to its practical import.

No empirical comparison against low-rank covariance VI (Tomczak et al., Swiatkowski et al.) or SWAG, and no empirical comparison against the Bayesian LoRA/Laplace-LoRA/Bella baselines that are discussed at length in Appendix A — despite these being the most directly comparable low-rank BNN methods. The paper's own limitations section acknowledges this gap.

Architectures tested remain small-scale (BERT-mini-sized 4-layer transformer, 2-layer LSTM, 2-layer MLP); the motivating claim that low-rank BNNs are needed for 'billions of parameters' modern models (Introduction) is never empirically tested at a scale where full-rank BNNs would actually become infeasible, leaving the central scalability claim only partially supported.

Low-Rank consistently underperforms Deep Ensembles on calibration (NLL, sometimes ECE) across all three main benchmarks; while the paper frames this as an OOD-detection/calibration tradeoff, no method or ablation is provided that closes this gap, and the proposed mitigation (ensembling multiple low-rank models) is left as untested future work.

The PAC-Bayes complexity ratio in Theorem 3.8 is stated with approximate ('≃') equalities that implicitly assume C_max is the same for full-rank and low-rank posteriors; this assumption is non-trivial (per-parameter KL can differ substantially between the two parameterizations) and is only properly caveated in an appendix remark (Remark D.5), not in the main text where the headline bound is presented.

Rank selection in practice relies on ablation studies with reduced budget rather than being derived from the paper's own generalization bounds, so the theory–practice link for the central design choice (choosing r) is weak; the bounds serve mainly as post-hoc validation rather than a predictive tool.

Several strong claims (e.g., 'no prior work trains low-rank BNNs end-to-end across diverse architectures with rigorous theoretical guarantees') are somewhat absolute and depend on how narrowly 'end-to-end' and 'diverse architectures' are defined relative to cited prior work.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are averaged over only 4-5 seeds, and the paper itself notes overlapping confidence intervals for some reported improvements (e.g., AUPR-OOD in Table 1), which tempers confidence in some of the finer-grained comparative claims.

strengths: The empirical evaluation spans three modalities (tabular MIMIC-III, time-series Beijing PM2.5, text SST-2) and three architecture families (MLP, LSTM, Transformer), which is more breadth than typical BNN papers.

The paper is unusually transparent about its own limitations (calibration gap vs. Deep Ensembles, overlapping confidence intervals, lack of SWAG/low-rank-covariance baselines, vacuous Gaussian complexity bounds), which is commendable scientific honesty even though these admissions undercut the paper's central claims.
The identification of a consistent calibration-vs-OOD-detection tradeoff across three independent experiments is a genuinely interesting empirical observation.
Reproducibility documentation (hardware, software versions, hyperparameters, initialization schemes) is thorough.

The attempt to connect Pinto et al.'s deterministic low-rank Gaussian-complexity bounds to the Bayesian posterior-mean predictor via convex-hull/closure invariance (Appendix E) is a technically careful, if narrow, contribution.
weaknesses: The headline theoretical result (Theorem 3.4, 'singularity' of the induced posterior) is a restatement of the elementary fact that rank-constrained matrices form a measure-zero algebraic variety; the extensive formal machinery (Lemmas 3.2-3.3, full proofs in Appendix B) dresses up a well-known and essentially unsurprising fact as a major geometric insight, inflating the paper's apparent theoretical depth without commensurate novelty.

The paper's own Section 3.5 and Figure 3 admit that the Gaussian-complexity bounds are 'vacuous for both methods and do not provide practical generalization certificates,' yet an entire 15-page appendix (Section E) is devoted to deriving and extending these bounds; this large theoretical apparatus contributes no actionable or empirically verified guarantee, which substantially weakens the claimed significance of the 'theory' contribution advertised in the abstract.

The PAC-Bayes comparison (Theorem 3.8) assumes equal per-parameter KL (Cmax) between full-rank and low-rank posteriors to derive the headline sqrt(r(m+n)/mn) complexity ratio; this assumption is not justified or empirically verified, and the 'general case' remark (Remark D.5) concedes the comparison can fail when per-parameter KLs differ, which is the realistic regime.

Empirically, the proposed method does not clearly dominate any baseline: it has worse NLL/ECE than Deep Ensembles in all three main experiments, is only 'second-best' or comparable to Full-Rank BBB on several core metrics (e.g., MIMIC AUROC ties Full-Rank at 0.895, both well below Deep Ensemble's 0.929), and the central claim of being 'competitive with 5-member Deep Ensembles' glosses over consistently worse calibration and in-domain discrimination.

The claimed computational efficiency benefit does not hold at the scales actually tested: Table 9 shows the low-rank MLP on MIMIC-III is slightly *slower* to train than Full-Rank BBB (532s vs 502s) despite 70% fewer parameters, directly contradicting the efficiency narrative; genuine speedups appear only for the one larger (and still modest, ~10M-parameter) Transformer experiment.

Despite extensive qualitative comparison to prior low-rank BNN methods in Appendix A (Bella/SVGD-LoRA, Laplace-LoRA, rank-1 multiplicative, low-rank covariance methods of Tomczak/Swiatkowski), none of these are included as empirical baselines except rank-1 multiplicative; the paper's claim of favorable positioning relative to this literature is argued only narratively, not empirically.

No comparison to other common lightweight/scalable uncertainty baselines (MC-Dropout, SWAG, Laplace approximation) is provided anywhere, despite these being standard, cheap alternatives directly relevant to the paper's efficiency claims; the limitations section itself flags this gap as something that 'would strengthen the positioning' but it is never addressed.

The architectures tested (128-unit MLP, 64-unit 2-layer LSTM, a 4-layer d_model=256 'BERT-mini'-style Transformer with ~10M parameters) are small by modern standards, undercutting the paper's framing (citing Papamarkou et al. 2024 and large-scale AI) that this method addresses scaling BNNs to 'modern architectures' with 'billions of parameters'; no evidence is given that the approach scales to truly large models.

Rank selection relies on reduced-budget ablation studies and single final rank choices per dataset with results reported for only one chosen configuration; the sensitivity analysis (Figures 10, 13, 14) shows substantial metric variation across nearby ranks, raising concerns about cherry-picking and about the robustness/reproducibility of the specific headline numbers.

The MSE-Lipschitz assumption underlying Theorems 3.6/3.7 requires bounded outputs (Remark C.10), a restrictive and not-always-satisfied condition for the regression tasks (Beijing PM2.5, toy regression) actually run, yet the paper does not verify or discuss whether this condition holds in those specific experiments.

The manuscript's extremely long appendix (65+ pages) devotes substantial space to proving elementary linear-algebra and probability facts (e.g., existence of rank factorizations, zero-sets of polynomials, covariance of independent products) that are textbook results, suggesting padding that obscures the genuinely novel contributions and makes it harder to assess the paper's real technical core.

strengths: Clean and well-motivated core idea (variational posterior on low-rank factors A,B rather than full W), clearly positioned against prior low-rank BNN approaches with a thorough comparison table and related work appendix.

Extensive and largely rigorous theoretical contributions: posterior singularity w.r.t. Lebesgue measure, EYM-based loss approximation/decomposition, PAC-Bayes complexity scaling as sqrt(r(m+n)/mn), and a non-trivial Gaussian-complexity transfer result bridging deterministic rank-sensitive bounds to Bayesian predictive means via convex-hull/closure invariance arguments.

Broad empirical evaluation spanning three architecture families (MLP, LSTM, Transformer) and multiple modalities (tabular/MIMIC-III, time-series/Beijing air quality, text/SST-2), plus additional vision and toy-regression experiments in the appendix.
Unusually honest reporting of trade-offs (e.g., consistent calibration vs. OOD-detection tradeoff relative to Deep Ensembles) rather than overselling results.
Principled, derived (not just heuristic) initialization scheme for low-rank variational layers, including variance-matching and SVD warm-start analysis.
Strong reproducibility documentation: hardware/software versions, seeds, hyperparameters, and training details are specified in detail.
weaknesses: The Gaussian-complexity bounds, while theoretically interesting, are explicitly shown to be vacuous in practice, limiting the practical payoff of a large portion (Section 3.5, Appendix E) of the theoretical contribution.

Empirical comparisons omit several of the most directly relevant low-rank covariance baselines that the paper itself discusses (e.g., SWAG, k-tied Normal, Tomczak et al.), limiting the strength of the main empirical claims.
Results rely on only 4-5 seeds per experiment with some overlapping confidence intervals (acknowledged by the authors), and no formal significance testing is reported.
Benchmarks remain relatively small-scale (e.g., BERT-mini-style 4-layer transformer, small MLP/LSTM), so claims about scalability to large modern architectures are not directly substantiated.

The paper and appendix are very long (65+ pages of appendix) relative to the core empirical contribution, with some sections (e.g., extensive high-probability spectral norm bound derivations) having limited practical impact on the reported results.
The explanation for the observed calibration-OOD detection tradeoff is largely qualitative/hand-wavy rather than tightly connected to the paper's own theoretical results.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning four architecture families (MLP, LSTM, Transformer) and diverse tasks (tabular clinical prediction, time series, text classification, plus MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/toy regression in the appendix), with multiple OOD datasets and multi-seed reporting.

Careful and largely rigorous appendix providing full proofs of all theoretical claims, detailed experimental protocols (hardware, seeds, hyperparameters), and controlled profiling benchmarks that isolate parameter/memory/runtime effects from confounds in end-to-end training time.

The extension of Pinto et al.'s deterministic Gaussian-complexity bounds to the Bayesian posterior-mean predictor via a convex-hull/closure argument (Section 3.5/Appendix E) is a genuine, non-trivial technical contribution that goes beyond simply restating PAC-Bayes.
Thorough related-work positioning against adjacent low-rank BNN literatures (rank-1 perturbations, low-rank covariance VI, Bayesian LoRA/Bella, Laplace-LoRA) with a clear comparison table.

Honest and detailed limitations discussion, including acknowledgment of overlapping confidence intervals, the calibration gap relative to Deep Ensembles, and supplementary SWAG/ensembling studies added to probe robustness of the main claims.
Practical initialization scheme (variance-matching, SVD warm-start) is theoretically motivated and empirically tested.
weaknesses: The central theoretical novelty, that a rank-r factorized posterior is singular w.r.t. Lebesgue measure, is a straightforward consequence of the pushforward of a lower-dimensional parameter space under a smooth map having measure zero; the extensive formal treatment (many appendix pages proving elementary facts such as zero sets of non-trivial polynomials having measure zero) does not add much conceptual insight beyond what is already intuitive, and the paper's narrative sometimes over-states the significance of this geometric fact as if it were a deep or previously unrecognized property.

The PAC-Bayes and Gaussian-complexity bounds are largely combinations/adaptations of existing results (McAllester 1998, Eckart-Young-Mirsky, Pinto et al. 2025) rather than fundamentally new theoretical machinery; the 'tighter bounds' framing compares complexity terms only, without addressing that empirical risk for the low-rank posterior is generally higher, so the net generalization comparison is not conclusively established.

Empirical results are mixed and do not consistently support a clear practical advantage: Deep Ensembles remain stronger on NLL/AUROC-OOD on SST-2 and on in-distribution AUROC/NLL on MIMIC-III; the paper's own 'calibration-OOD tradeoff' framing effectively concedes that no single metric is uniformly improved, which weakens the claimed practical significance of the singular low-rank posterior.

Missing direct empirical comparison against more recent/competitive low-rank Bayesian baselines discussed in Appendix A (Bella, LoRA+Bayes/Laplace-LoRA, low-rank covariance VI) — these are only discussed qualitatively, not benchmarked, despite being the closest prior art.

Assumption E.4 (almost-sure spectral-norm bounds on factors) required for Theorem 3.9 is unrealistic for standard unbounded Gaussian variational posteriors; the high-probability relaxations in Appendix E.10–E.11 add substantial additional machinery and an extra convexity assumption on the loss, suggesting the core theorem as stated in the main text does not directly apply to the Gaussian posteriors used in the experiments.

Rank selection relies on ad hoc ablation with reduced compute budget rather than a principled or automatic procedure, which is acknowledged but leaves a meaningful practical gap, especially since Figures 10/13/14 show the rank choice materially shifts the calibration-OOD tradeoff.

The paper is extremely long (70-page appendix) with substantial redundancy and over-formalization of minor lemmas, which dilutes focus on the paper's genuinely novel contributions and may hinder reviewer/reader ability to verify all claims carefully.

strengths: The core idea (treating low-rank variational factors as inducing a singular posterior on the rank-r manifold) is a clean geometric reframing that connects classical low-rank BNN work to measure-theoretic language and to PAC-Bayes/Gaussian-complexity bounds.

Extensive empirical coverage across MLP (MIMIC-III), LSTM (Beijing Air Quality), and Transformer (SST-2) architectures with OOD, calibration, and selective-prediction metrics, plus supplementary SWAG and ensembling studies.

The appendix provides very long, explicit derivations (singularity proofs, EYM-based loss bounds, PAC-Bayes bound, Gaussian-complexity transfer via convex-hull/closure arguments) which at least makes the claims auditable.

Honest and fairly thorough limitations discussion, including acknowledgment that Deep Ensembles remain stronger on several in-distribution likelihood metrics and that confidence intervals sometimes overlap.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim ("singularity" of the induced posterior) is a nearly trivial measure-theory fact — any pushforward of a continuous distribution through a low-dimensional parameterization (e.g., any neural network output distribution, any manifold-constrained reparameterization) is singular w.r.t. Lebesgue measure on the ambient space. This is dressed up with heavy formalism (Definitions, Lemmas, a full proof of 'zero sets of polynomials have measure zero') but carries essentially no new statistical content beyond 'rank-r matrices form a measure-zero set,' which is textbook. The paper oversells this as a core theoretical contribution and uses it as the title and major framing device.

The PAC-Bayes bound (Theorem 3.8) is just a routine substitution of parameter count into McAllester's bound; the 'tighter bound' claim is simply restating that r(m+n) < mn when r is small, which is already obvious from the parameter-count argument and requires no new theory. Similarly the Eckart-Young-Mirsky-based loss bounds (3.6, 3.7) are direct corollaries of Lipschitz continuity plus the classical EYM theorem — not novel.

The Gaussian-complexity transfer argument (Section E) is the most technically substantive part, but it rests on a strong almost-sure spectral-norm-bound assumption (Assumption E.4) that standard Gaussian variational posteriors violate; the paper's own high-probability 'fixes' (Section E.10) require an additional convexity assumption on the loss and introduce extra slack terms, undermining the claimed bound's direct applicability to the actual Gaussian posteriors used in experiments.

Empirically, the method's story is inconsistent and somewhat cherry-picked: Deep Ensembles are frequently better on NLL and in-domain discrimination; the paper calls this a 'calibration-OOD tradeoff' but the explanations offered are post-hoc narrative rather than tied back to the theory (e.g., the EYM bounds and PAC-Bayes bounds give no quantitative prediction matching the observed tradeoffs). The theory and experiments are largely disconnected: no result predicts when/why low-rank should win at OOD detection but lose at calibration.

Only 3 main benchmark tasks (one dataset per architecture family) with 4-5 seeds; rank selection via extensive ablation plus optional SVD-decay 'validation' raises concerns about implicit hyperparameter searching/overfitting to test-set-adjacent OOD splits, especially since the OOD sets (newborns, Guangzhou, AG News) are somewhat convenient choices and the AUPR/AUROC-OOD gains are not always statistically decisive (explicitly acknowledged: 'some confidence intervals overlap').

The paper is extremely long and padded with over 70 pages of appendix (multiple near-redundant subsections, exhaustive restatements, extensive 'remarks' and 'interpretations' after every lemma) relative to the genuinely new content, which is a presentation weakness and makes it hard to assess what the paper's real, defensible contribution is versus repackaged standard results.

The comparison table (Table 5, Appendix A) and relevant baselines (rank-1, low-rank covariance, LoRA-Bayes variants) are only discussed qualitatively; no direct empirical comparison against Swiatkowski et al. or Tomczak et al.'s low-rank-covariance VI (arguably the most relevant competing approach) is provided, despite these being highlighted as a key related category in the introduction.

Practical significance is undercut by the reported wall-clock results: at small/medium scale (MIMIC-III, Beijing) the factorized layers show negligible or even negative training-time benefits despite large nominal parameter savings, limiting the 'efficiency' claim to large Transformer-scale settings only.

strengths: Theoretical contribution is substantial and carefully executed: the singularity result (Thm 3.4) is simple but correctly formalizes an intuitive but previously informal observation; the PAC-Bayes complexity reduction (Thm 3.8), EYM-based loss decomposition (Thm 3.6/3.7), and especially the Gaussian-complexity transfer from deterministic to Bayesian predictive means via convex-hull/closure invariance (Prop E.13, Thm 3.9) are non-trivial and rigorously proved, with full proofs in the appendix.

Honest and nuanced empirical reporting: the paper does not oversell results, explicitly stating that Deep Ensembles retain advantages on in-domain NLL/accuracy in several settings (SST-2, MIMIC-III) and characterizing a genuine calibration-vs-OOD-detection tradeoff rather than claiming uniform superiority.

Broad and non-trivial implementation effort: the method is implemented from scratch (not via black-box libraries) across three distinct architecture families (MLP, LSTM with weight caching per Fortunato et al., Transformer with batch-sparse embeddings), each requiring different engineering solutions, which is a genuine contribution to reproducibility and demonstrates the method's generality.

Extensive and rigorous empirical validation: four real datasets with meaningful OOD shifts (adult→newborn ICU, Beijing→Guangzhou climate, SST-2→AGNews domain shift), multiple seeds with reported variance, additional comparisons to SWAG, a 5-member low-rank ensemble ablation, controlled profiling benchmarks isolating peak memory/epoch time from end-to-end training time, and three additional controlled experiments (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, toy regression) that cleanly isolate uncertainty-quantification behavior.

Thorough treatment of practical caveats, including an entire appendix section (E.10-E.11) addressing the gap between the almost-sure spectral norm assumption needed for the Gaussian-complexity proof and realistic unbounded Gaussian posteriors, with concrete high-probability relaxations and concentration bounds (Van Handel).

Clear comparative positioning against related low-rank BNN literature (rank-1 perturbations, low-rank covariance approximations, Bayesian LoRA variants, matrix factorization, compression) with a structured table clarifying genuine distinctions in support geometry and parameterization.
weaknesses: The headline 'singularity' framing (Section 3.1) is conceptually straightforward (rank-deficient matrices form a measure-zero set) and somewhat oversold as a central conceptual contribution relative to its actual explanatory power for the empirical results; the paper would be stronger framed primarily around the PAC-Bayes/Gaussian-complexity contributions and the empirical findings.

Several empirical conclusions rest on small numbers of seeds (4-5) with visibly overlapping confidence intervals on some key metrics (acknowledged by the authors, e.g., Table 1 AUPR-OOD), which limits the strength of claims about consistent superiority in OOD detection.

The three benchmark tasks, while real-world, are all relatively small-scale (MLPs/LSTMs/tiny 4-layer Transformers on datasets with tens of thousands of examples); the paper's motivation explicitly invokes scaling BNNs to billion-parameter modern architectures, but no experiments approach that regime, leaving the central scalability claim only partially substantiated.

The Gaussian-complexity transfer result (Theorem 3.9) requires an almost-sure spectral-norm bound on the posterior factors (Assumption E.4) that does not hold for the Gaussian posteriors actually used in the experiments; while high-probability relaxations are discussed at length in the appendix, the main paper does not flag this gap, and it is unclear whether the enforcement mechanisms (projection/clipping) were actually used in the reported experiments.

The practical difference between the proposed method and known techniques (low-rank factorized VI, essentially combining LoRA-style factorization with mean-field VI from initialization) is more incremental than the number of theoretical claims might suggest; the core algorithmic novelty is the application and bound derivation rather than a fundamentally new inference procedure.

Rank and KL-weight selection require per-task ablation/tuning without a fully automated procedure, and the 'singular value decay' validation step requires a pretrained deterministic model, creating some tension with the claim of being a purely end-to-end method independent of pretrained backbones.

Comparisons to low-rank covariance approaches (Tomczak et al., 2020; Swiatkowski et al., 2020) are discussed only qualitatively in Appendix A rather than empirically benchmarked, despite being arguably the closest prior art in spirit.
